A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TokenTiming study. Their main text, algorithms, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: V3 reports original decoding experiments across 25 model pairs, including throughput, acceptance rates, task-specific speedups, and additional appendix analyses.

after.justification: V4 retains the original benchmark and domain-specific results and adds a constructed-prompt tokenization alignment case study in Section 5.2.8.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 retain the same re-tokenization, DTW alignment, window constraint, verification, and prefix-update procedures. Appendix A retains the same probability assignments for both mapping cases. The newly explicit top-1 limitation documents the mechanism without establishing a procedural change.

E1.justification: V3's separate six-language evaluation in Appendix O is removed, substantially narrowing evaluated linguistic coverage. V4 adds a constructed special-symbol prompt scenario using WordPiece and BPE in Section 5.2.8. The Spec-Bench tasks and medical/code domain evaluations remain.

E2.justification: AR and TLI remain the main comparators; Figure 4 retains Medusa and EAGLE-1/2/3, and the domain-specific comparison retains TLI. RDK remains excluded from evaluation. Changes in model-name capitalization and abbreviation do not change comparator membership.

E3.justification: The new fragmentation case constructs special-symbol inputs and compares their WordPiece/BPE alignment. V3's adaptive and fixed four/eight-candidate testing procedures are no longer reported. Retained benchmark settings, including 480 generations, 25 model pairs, generation hyperparameters, and approximately 15% repetition exclusion, are unchanged.

E4.justification: V3's candidate-length and acceptance-trajectory analysis in Appendix C/Figures 7–9 and its language-specific alignment analysis in Appendix O/Figure 13 are removed. V4 adds a single constructed-prompt robustness case in Section 5.2.8. Window-size sensitivity, runtime-overhead, and repetition analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeat counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The retained results continue to use point estimates without added uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V4 removes multilingual speedups, including French 2.23× and Chinese 1.06× from v3 Table 11, candidate/accepted-token trajectories, and absolute vocabulary/intersection counts from Tables 9–10. It adds the terminal-token alignment finding in Figure 8. Main Tables 1–2, retained speedup plots, and domain-specific scores are unchanged; the repetition heatmap preserves v3's numerical entries.

T1.justification: V4 deletes Appendix A.3's general acceptance/rejection losslessness derivation, including the residual sampling distribution and final target-distribution identity. It retains the string-consistency lemma and two probability-mapping cases without a replacement general proof. V3's candidate-length equations in Appendix C.1 are also absent.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the claims of lossless acceleration across heterogeneous vocabularies, off-the-shelf drafts without retraining, and the headline 1.57× and 2.27× speedups. Wording changes do not materially alter these claims.

C2.justification: V4 explicitly identifies top-1 probability transfer and character-based alignment as limitations and interprets the new fragmented-tokenization example as evidence of robustness. V3's detailed language-specific applicability explanation and special-token misalignment discussion are removed, although a broader language-granularity caveat remains.

D1.justification: V4 no longer documents v3 Appendix C's candidate-length bounds and confidence filtering or Appendix J's special-token removal, prefix shortening, and tokenizer-specific table. These are consequential losses of reproduction information. V4 newly states top-1 transfer and describes UTF8 handling; hardware, retained generation hyperparameters, and the code link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V4 adds Sennrich et al. (2016) and Wang et al. (2019) for the new tokenization discussion and removes Kudo and Richardson (2018). The broader positioning against homogeneous, pruned-vocabulary, and heterogeneous speculative decoding remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V4 copyedits prose, standardizes model names, replaces Δid with Δpos, simplifies method subsection titles, and clarifies the DQwen abbreviation. It shortens the generated-text example and adds dedicated limitations, ethics, and acknowledgements sections. The retained main exposition and appendix sequence largely preserve their previous organization.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 replace colored highlighting and arrows with boldface, several diagrams and plots are restyled, and v3 Table 3 becomes the equivalent repetition heatmap in v4 Figure 7. V4 adds Figure 8, removes candidate-length and multilingual displays, vocabulary/tokenizer tables, and one trace panel, and relocates retained figures.

improvement.justification: Copyediting, explicit limitations, and the new fragmentation case offer benefits. However, removing the general losslessness derivation, candidate-generation and special-token preprocessing details, and multilingual evidence substantially reduces theoretical documentation, reproducibility, and evidence about applicability. These losses concern the paper's unchanged universal, lossless-acceleration claims and outweigh the presentation improvements and limited new case study.
